attributes.title: Level 6

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use comments to create multiple sections in the editor to better organize your code?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What code might be placed underneath each comment?

❓ How do you create blank lines in the JavaScript editor?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that typing // tells the project to skip over the text that follows and move onto the next line of code. Just as when naming sprites, it’s useful to be short and descriptive when writing comments. 

💡 Encourage the ninja to use best practices when adding comments to their code. It’s helpful to space out comments in the editor, so that code can be placed in the lines between them. They can use the Enter key to create blank lines between comments. They should also add a space after the slashes in the comment, before adding the text.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by adding code comments to organize where the code will go in the editor!


Add comments with these descriptions to the project: game set up, sprite set up, game mechanics, on countdown end.


Start each comment with // and add several blank lines between each comment.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select the basketball court image as the background, then use the paint editor to change its colors?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What colors might be used to change the appearance of the basketball court image?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to use the fill tool in the editor to change the color of large sections on the basketball court image.
steps.instructions:
Add the basketball court background image to the project.


Open Scene, drag [set background image to (img)] under // game set up.


Click the palette to open the paint editor, then click My Assets at the top of the screen to select the basketball court background image. Use the paint editor to customize the colors of the court.


Click ▶ to see the basketball court background image appear on the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the hoop sprite to appear along the top center and the player sprite to appear along the bottom center of the screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What positions might you set each sprite to, so that the player sprite appears at the bottom center of the screen and the hoop sprite appears at the top center?

❓ What might happen to the player and hoop sprites in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they can always toggle back to blocks to use the coordinate grid to select a sprite’s position on screen.
steps.instructions:
Create 2 sprites to add a player and a hoop to the project.


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] underneath // sprite set up. Click the palette to open the paint editor, then click My Assets at the top of the screen to select the basketball hoop image. Name the sprite hoopSprite. Repeat this process to create a playerSprite, choosing a person sprite from the gallery as its image.


Set both sprites’ positions by opening Sprites and dragging [set (mySprite) position to x y] underneath the code that creates each sprite. Update the sprite’s name and the x (0-160) and y (0-120) parameters in each line of code so that the hoop appears along the top center and the player sprite appears along the bottom center of the screen. 


Click ▶ to see the player and hoop sprites appear on screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the player sprite to only move left and right on the screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What directions is the player sprite able to move in? How do you know?

❓ What symbol should be used to separate the parameters in the moveSprite function?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the Ninja to use the documentation to add the vx and vy parameters in the moveSprite function and to use commas , to separate the arguments.
steps.instructions:
Allow the player sprite to move horizontally across the screen.


Open Controller and drag [move (mySprite) with buttons] underneath the player sprite’s existing code. Replace mySprite with playerSprite, then type a comma , and 100 to set the vx parameter, followed by another comma and 0 to set the vy parameter, so the player sprite can only move left and right.


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) stay in screen (true)] underneath the player sprite’s existing code. Update the player sprite’s name, and use the default argument true so the sprite will stay in screen.


Click ▶ then use the direction buttons to test the player sprite’s movement.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the ball sprite’s x position to a random integer between 10 and screen.width-10?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where will the ball sprite appear on the screen? How do you know?

❓ Why might it be useful to use the screen.width -10 to set the position for a sprite?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Walk the ninja through the logic of the ball sprite’s position code. The ball sprite will always appear at the same y position as the player sprite. Its x position will be randomly selected from a range between 10 - 170 (screen.width (180) -10). By subtracting 10 from the screen width, the ninja is ensuring that the ball sprite will be visible at all positions and will not be cut off by the screen edges.
steps.instructions:
Add a ball sprite that appears at random x values to the project.


Underneath // sprite set up, add code to create a ballSprite and set its position. Set the sprite’s image to the basketball image in My Assets.


To keep the ball from appearing out of bounds, set the x position to a randint between 10 and screen.width - 10. Then set the y position to the same value as the player sprite’s y position.


Click ▶ to see the ball sprite appear at a random x value along the bottom of the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the ball sprite to follow the hoop sprite at a random speed?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What will happen when the player sprite overlaps the ball sprite?

❓ How can you use code to make the player sprite appear to be shooting the ball towards the hoop?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja why they are placing code under // game mechanics This section of code will tell the rules of the game and what the player needs to do to play. In this step, the ninja will code the first rule: the player sprite needs to overlap the ball sprite, in order to throw it towards the hoop sprite.

💡 Prompt the ninja to notice how setting the ball sprite to follow the hoop sprite at a random speed makes it appear as if the ball is being thrown towards the hoop. Ask the ninja to consider other ways that they might achieve the same effect in JavaScript.
steps.instructions:
Code the player to throw the ball towards the hoop!


Open Loops and drag [run code forever] under // game mechanics. Then open Logic and drag [if] inside the curly brackets { } of the forever loop.


Delete true inside the parentheses of the if condition. Open Sprites and drag [(mySprite) overlaps with (otherSprite)] inside the parentheses of the if condition. Replace mySprite with playerSprite and otherSprite with ballSprite.


Open Sprites and drag [set (myEnemy) follow (mySprite)] inside the curly brackets { } of the if condition. Replace myEnemy with ballSprite and mySprite with hoopSprite. In the parentheses, add a random speed parameter by typing , then use a randint value between 50-100 to set the speed the ball moves towards the hoop.


Click ▶ then move the player sprite to overlap the ball sprite to throw it towards the hoop.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use a Boolean AND operator to run code if the player sprite overlaps the ball sprite AND the A button is pressed?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is using a Boolean AND operator in JavaScript similar and different to the blocks editor?

❓ Why is using a Boolean AND operator helpful when more than one condition needs to be true, in order for code to run? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that they will need to press Shift + 7 on their keyboard to type the & symbol.

💡 Help the ninja make the connection between the Boolean AND operator in JavaScript and the <and> Boolean in the blocks editor. Both allow a different value to be placed on either side. When placed in a conditional, the Boolean AND operator requires both conditions to be true in order for the code to run.
steps.instructions:
Code the player to only throw the ball when the A button is pressed.


To throw the ball when the player sprite overlaps the ball sprite AND the A button is pressed, type 2 “and” signs && inside the parentheses of the if condition after the overlapsWith function. The double “and” sign (&&) is called a Boolean AND operator.


Then, open Controller and drag [is button (button) pressed] inside the parentheses on the right side of &&. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: controller.A.isPressed(). Use the default property A.


Now, the ball sprite will only move towards the hoop if the player sprite overlaps with the ball sprite AND the A button is pressed.


Click ▶ then use the A button to test this out!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the ball sprite to unfollow the hoop sprite, then use copy (Ctrl + C) and paste (Ctrl + V) to reset its position?
steps.instructions:
Reset the ball sprite after making the shot!


Open Logic and drag a second [if] inside the curly brackets { } of the forever loop, underneath the other conditional.


Delete true inside the parentheses of the if condition. Open Sprites and drag [(mySprite) overlaps with (otherSprite)] inside the parentheses then update mySprite with ballSprite and otherSprite with hoopSprite.


Pause the ball sprite’s movement before it resets to a new position. Open Loops and drag a [pause (100) ms] inside the curly brackets { } of the if statement, then update the time parameter to 500. Open Sprites and drag [set (this) unfollow] underneath.  Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: myEnemy.unfollow()


Replace myEnemy with ballSprite so the ball sprite stops following the hoop sprite.


Find and copy (Ctrl + C) the ball sprite’s setPosition code, then paste (Ctrl + V) the code inside the if statement to set a new position for the ball sprite.


Click ▶ to see the ball sprite reset to a different position after making a basket.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you declare a new variable, then use an addition assignment operator to increase the variable by 1, after the ball sprite overlaps the hoop sprite?
steps.instructions:
Use a variable to keep track of how many baskets the player makes!


Under // game set up, type let and the variable name, throwsMade. Then, use an assignment operator = to assign the value 0 to the variable.


Under // game mechanics, type the name of the variable on the first line inside the if statement that checks if the ball overlaps with the hoop. Then, type an addition assignment operator += and a value of 1, so that the code reads: throwsMade += 1


Now, the project will count how many times the ball sprite overlaps the hoop sprite.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the countdown to a short amount of time in info.startCountdown, then use quotation marks to separate the strings from the variables in showLongText?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you place strings in quotation marks, use plus signs + to join, or concatenate, variables, and space words out correctly?

❓ How is the throwsMade variable used to tell the user how many baskets were scored in the project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that concatenation means joining multiple strings and/or variables in order.

💡 Point out to the ninja that this dialog box should share how many baskets were scored by the end of the project. Consequently, they should play the project, read the message, and make sure that each string and variable is placed correctly to communicate this information.

💡 Prompt the ninja to notice that the variable name used in the code turns into its value when the dialog box appears. This is a useful way to share stored data back to the user in a project.
steps.instructions:
Set a countdown timer, then reveal the player’s score when the timer reaches 0!


Open Info and drag [start countdown (10) (s)] under // game set up, then update the time parameter so that the user only has a short amount of time to shoot baskets.


Open Info and drag [run code on countdown end] under // on countdown end. Then, open Game and drag [show long text (str) (layout)] inside the curly brackets { } of onCountdownEnd. 


In the parentheses, replace null with a string, such as “Wow! You made “, then type + to join, or concatenate, the value of the throwsMade variable to the first string. Type another + then complete the message with another string, such as “ baskets. That’s impressive!”. Update the DialogLayout property, too.


Click ▶ to see the number of baskets made appear on screen after the timer runs out.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use a relational operator >= to run code if the number of baskets is greater than or equal to a certain value?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is using a relational operator >= in JavaScript similar and different to the blocks editor?

❓ What condition needs to be true, in order for the code in the if condition to run?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The relational operator >= checks if the value on the left is greater than or equal to the value on the right. Point out the connection to the <0=0> comparison blocks in the blocks editor to the ninja. In this comparison block, the ninja could select the greater than or equal to symbol >= to check if a value was greater than or equal to another.

💡 Walk the ninja through the logic of the if conditional. At the end of the countdown, if the player has made greater than or equal to 6 baskets, then a dialog box shows telling the user how many total baskets they made.
steps.instructions:
Challenge the player to make a certain number of baskets before the timer runs out!


Open Logic and drag [if] inside the curly brackets { } of onCountdownEnd. Replace true inside the parentheses of the if condition with a condition that checks if the value of throwsMade is greater than or equal to a certain number.


Type >= to create a relational operator that checks if the value on the left is greater than or equal to the value on the right. Then, add a value to set as the goal number of baskets, so that the code looks like: throwsMade >= 6 


Cut (Ctrl + X) the showLongText code and paste (Ctrl + V) it inside the curly brackets { } of the if condition.


Last, open Game and drag [reset game] under the conditional to start the game over again.


Click ▶ to see the dialog box message that appears after the timer runs out if the score is greater than or equal to a certain number.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you subtract the value of the variable from the goal score?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja: 

❓ Did you use a plus sign (+) to concatenate the string and the value of the variable subtracted from the goal number of points, to display a sentence?

❓ What condition needs to be true, in order for the code in the else condition to run?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that they can use math operations, such as subtraction, to incorporate user input and share information back to the user, comparing it to another value from the project. 

💡 At the end of the countdown, if the player has not made greater than or equal to 6 baskets, a dialog box will show telling the user how many more baskets they needed to make in order to win.
steps.instructions:
Tell the player how many baskets they missed by.


Type else { } after the closing curly bracket of the if condition. Place the cursor inside the curly brackets, then create a blank line after the else condition. Use another showLongText to create a dialog box with a string, such as “Almost! You needed “ + then the variable subtracted from the goal score in parentheses: (6 - throwsMade) 


Type another + then complete the message with another string, such as “ more baskets to win.”. Update the DialogLayout property, too.


Click ▶ to see the different dialog box messages that appear after the timer runs out.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add directions so that the user knows they need to overlap the player sprite with the hoop sprite and press the A button in order to shoot the ball?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What directions might tell the user how to play the game? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that since 2 conditions must be true in order for the player sprite to shoot the ball, they should include a note about the conditions in the directions.
steps.instructions:
Finish the project by adding game directions!


Open Game and drag [show long text (str) (layout)] onto a blank line underneath the code to set the background image. Update the string and layout parameters, so that the dialog box shares directions for the user to follow.


Click ▶ to play the completed project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a project in JavaScript that uses Boolean operators to throw a basketball towards the hoop when the player overlaps the ball and presses the A button.

validationItems.text: Create a player sprite, set its position, move it with the controller, and keep it in the screen.
Create a hoop sprite and set its position.
Create a ball sprite and set its position to a random value.

Use a conditional statement inside a forever loop to check if the ball and player sprites overlap and the A button is pressed. If the condition evaluates to true, set the ball sprite to follow the hoop sprite.

Use a conditional statement inside a forever loop to check if the ball overlaps with the hoop. If the condition evaluates to true, pause the game, stop the ball from following the hoop, and reset its position.
Create a variable that is initialized to a value of 0 and is incremented when the ball sprite overlaps with the hoop sprite. Use >= to check the value of the variable in an if statement.
Use a countdown timer. When the timer ends, display a long text message and reset the game.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 6 of Blue Belt! Before you create your final Blue Belt project, there are a few neat tricks to learn that could take your game to the next level!
